respondents identify a series as the same thing under the same circumstances and probably by the same people; the number of incidents in the series is recorded; only one detailed victim module is completed based on the most recent incident.
one detailed module does not describe every incident in a series; series classification depends on respondent reporting.
from 1981 the first five incidents of a series were included in estimates; the cap reduced year-to-year sample variability; the approach supported a more stable time series.
historical stability was achieved by excluding higher-order incidents; pre-change estimates are not directly comparable with the revised method.

the five-incident cap could lower estimates for crime types such as violence; high-order repeat victimisation could be concentrated in subgroups; ONS cites sustained victimisation by a partner or family member as a potential measurement-error concern.
the limitation does not quantify every subgroup effect; historical and revised series require explicit break metadata.
ONS commissioned a review of high-frequency repeat-victimisation methods in 2015; the review was completed in spring 2016; users were consulted between July and September 2016.
review chronology is not a measurement result; implemented methodology must be distinguished from proposals considered.

the arbitrary cap of five was replaced by crime-specific imputation; the maximum is based on the 98th percentile of victim incident counts; percentiles are calculated from three-year rolling datasets.
the maximum varies by crime type and reference period; edition-specific percentile tables are required.

for many crime types the calculated 98th percentile is below five; ONS does not lower the maximum below five in those cases; incidents above the percentile can therefore remain included when the percentile is below five.
the rule is not a universal five-incident cap; crime-specific implementation must be read from the current table.
violence estimates are noticeably affected by the 98th-percentile method; criminal-damage estimates are also noticeably affected; most other crime types show smaller effects.
method effect is not evidence of a real-world crime change; affected categories still require confidence intervals.

98th-percentile values are more variable for children aged 10 to 15 than for adults; the child survey has a different sample structure; child and adult repeat-victimisation thresholds should not be pooled.
greater variability does not invalidate child estimates; child-specific editions and uncertainty remain necessary.
the numinc weight is used for calculating incidents; it is distinct from the core individual weight; incident and prevalence calculations therefore use different weighting roles.
numinc is not a general person weight; weight formulas are edition dependent.
the revised method included adjustments to survey design weights; the adjustments reduce variance in weights; the purpose was to lessen volatility in survey estimates.
variance reduction does not remove sampling or measurement error; old and revised weighting systems require separate metadata.
self-completion modules cover domestic abuse; they also cover sexual assault and stalking; other modules include drug use drinking gangs and personal security.
module availability can vary by survey edition; different topics can use different denominators.
sensitive questions are completed privately on a tablet; the design is intended to increase respondent comfort; privacy and confidentiality are central reasons for self-completion.
privacy design does not eliminate under-reporting; mode and safeguarding rules must be retained.

the domestic-abuse trial used a split sample; half received existing questions and half received new questions; respondents receiving new questions did not receive the existing sexual-assault and stalking questions in that module space.
trial arms have different available variables; combined estimates require explicit questionnaire routing.
new questions were designed for estimates since age 16; they were also designed for last-year estimates; reference periods are separately defined.
lifetime and last-year measures are not interchangeable; recall and exposure periods differ.
the questionnaire has separate partner and family sections; each section asks about abusive behaviours; the design also asks about impacts of those behaviours.
